**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 107, verses 1–7:**

Sūrat al-Māʿūn, and it has seven verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Religion?﴾ ﴿That is the one who repulses the orphan,﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the poor.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who pray,﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ ﴿who make a show [of their deeds],﴾ ﴿and withhold [simple] assistance.﴾

Sahā ʿan kadhā yashū sahwan: he neglected it and left it out of heedlessness. Al-Māʿūn is on the pattern fāʿūl, derived from al-maʿn, which means a small amount. The Arabs say: mā lahu maʿn, meaning "he has a little." Quṭrub said this. It is also said that its origin is maʿūna, and the alif replaces the hāʾ. Its original pattern is then mafʿal, as in makram, with the mīm being an added letter. After the alif has been added in place of the hāʾ, its pattern becomes māfʿul. It is also said that it is an ism mafʿūl from aʿāna yuʿīnu, formed on the pattern of mafʿūl. Its ʿayn was transposed to the place of the fāʾ, so it became mawʿūn. Then the wāw was changed to an alif, as they said in bawaba, "bāb," so it became māʿūn. On this view its pattern is mafʿūl.

Abū ʿUbayda, al-Zajjāj and al-Mubarrad said: in the pre-Islamic period, al-māʿūn was everything that has benefit in it, even to the point of the axe, the bucket, the cooking pot and the firestarter, and everything that has benefit, whether little or much. They cited the verse of al-Aʿshā:

*With [a gift] more generous than his māʿūn, when their sky did not cloud over.*

They said: its meaning in Islam is obedience. The views of the exegetes on it will come, God willing, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Religion?﴾ ﴿That is the one who repulses the orphan,﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the poor.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who pray,﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ ﴿who make a show [of their deeds],﴾ ﴿and withhold [simple] assistance.﴾

This surah is Meccan according to the majority. It is Medinan according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda. Hibat Allāh, the blind exegete, said: half of it was revealed in Mecca concerning al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, and half in Medina concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the hypocrite. When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings upon the Quraysh, who did not believe in the resurrection and the recompense, He followed His favour to them with a warning of the recompense and a frightening of them with His punishment. It was revealed concerning Abū Jahl, or al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, or al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, or ʿUmar ibn ʿĀʾidh, or two men among the hypocrites, or Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, who used to slaughter a camel every week. An orphan came to him and asked him for something, and he struck him with a stick. These are views, the last of which is that of Ibn Jurayj.

The apparent sense is that *araʾayta* (have you seen) here means "tell me," so it takes two objects. The first is *alladhī* (the one who), and the second is omitted. Al-Ḥawfī supposed it to be: "Is he not deserving of God's punishment?" Al-Zamakhsharī supposed it to be: "Who is he?" That it means "tell me" is shown by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, *araʾaytuka* with the second-person kāf, since the kāf of address does not attach to the sense of seeing. Al-Ḥawfī said: it is also possible that it is from the seeing of the eye, so there would be no omission in the sentence. The interrogative hamza indicates affirmation and making understood, so that the listener may recall whoever is known to him with this description.

Al-dīn (the Religion) means the recompense, by reward and punishment. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is, "Have you recognised the one who denies the recompense? It is he who *repulses the orphan*," that is, pushes him away violently, with harshness or harm. "*And does not urge*," that is, does not stir his household to give food to the poor. He made the knowledge of denying the recompense the cause of withholding kindness and proceeding to harm the weak. End of quote.

The majority read *yadhuʿʿu* with a damma on the dāl and a shadda on the ʿayn. ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ and al-Yamānī read it with a fatḥa on the dāl and no shadda on the ʿayn, meaning he abandons him, that is, does not treat him well and is harsh with him. The majority read *wa-lā yaḥuḍḍu* as the present tense of ḥaḍḍa. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *yuḥāḍḍu*, the present of ḥāḍaḍtu.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: *bi-l-dīn* means "by the judgment of God." Mujāhid said: "by the reckoning." It is also said: "by the recompense," and it is said: "by the Qurʾān." Ibrāhīm ibn ʿArafa said: *yadhuʿʿu al-yatīm* means he pushes him away from his right. Mujāhid said: he pushes him away from his right and does not feed him. In the phrase *wa-lā yaḥuḍḍu* there is an indication that he himself does not feed, once it is assumed, and this is of the category of the more fitting, since if he does not urge others out of stinginess, then it is more fitting and more worthy that he himself abandon it in action. In the addition of *ṭaʿām* (food) to *al-miskīn* (the poor) there is evidence that the poor man is entitled to it.

When He first mentioned the pillar of disbelief, which is denying the Religion, He mentioned what follows from it of what relates to the Creator, which is worshipping Him through prayer, and He said: *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn* (so woe to those who pray). The apparent meaning is that those who pray are other than those previously mentioned. It is said: they are the one who repulses the orphan and not the one who urges. It is also said that each of the blameworthy attributes arises from denying the Religion. So *al-muṣallūn* here, and God knows best, are the hypocrites, to whom prayer is ascribed, meaning the outward forms they perform. Then He said: *alladhīna hum ʿan ṣalātihim sāhūn* (who are heedless of their prayer), considering that they do not perform it as the Muslim performs it, with belief in its obligation and drawing near to God through it. In a hadith concerning *ʿan ṣalātihim sāhūn*: "They delay it beyond its time out of contempt for it." Mujāhid said: it is delay of abandonment and neglect. Ibrāhīm said: it is the one who, when he prostrates, says "with his head like this," turning aside. Qatāda said: it is leaving it, or they are the heedless who do not care whether one of them has prayed or not. Quṭrub said: it is the one who does not settle down and does not remember God, exalted is He. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the hypocrites leave off prayer in secret and perform it openly. *And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily* (Qurʾān 4:142). This shows that it refers to the hypocrites.

His saying, exalted is He: *alladhīna hum yurāʾūn* (who make a show), and this is what Ibn Wahb reported from Mālik. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if He had said *fī ṣalātihim* (in their prayer), it would have applied to the believers. ʿAṭāʾ said: praise be to God, who said *ʿan ṣalātihim* and did not say *fī ṣalātihim*.

Al-Zamakhsharī said, after he had put forward, in what we have quoted from his words, what indicates that *fa-dhālika alladhī yadhuʿʿu* is in the place of the nominative: he said: another way is that *fa-dhālika* is a conjunction with *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, either as the conjunction of one essence to another essence, or as the conjunction of an attribute to an attribute. The answer to *araʾayta* would be omitted, because what follows indicates it. As if he said: "Tell me, and what do you say of one who denies the recompense, and of one who harms the orphan and does not feed the poor? Is what he does good?" Then He said: *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn*, that is, if it is known that he is evil, *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn*, in the sense of: "woe to them." But He put their description in the place of their pronoun, because they were, along with denying, and what was added to them, heedless of prayer, showing off, and not paying the zakat on their wealth. If you say: how did you make *al-muṣallīn* stand in place of the pronoun of *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, when it is singular? I say: its meaning is plural, because what is meant by it is the genus. End of quote.

So he made *fa-dhālika* in the place of the accusative, as a conjunction with the object. This is a strange construction, like your saying: "I honoured the one who visits us, that is the one who treats us well." What comes first to the mind is that *fa-dhālika* is nominative by being the subject. On the reading of the accusative the sense would be: "I honoured the one who visits us, so I honoured that one who treats us well." The demonstrative in this reading is not as firmly placed as the eloquent usage would have it, since there is no need to point to "the one who visits us." Rather, the eloquent form is "I honoured the one who visits us, so the one who treats us well," or "I honoured the one who visits us, so he treats us well." As for his saying "the conjunction of one essence to another essence," this is not correct, because *fa-dhālika* is a reference to *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, so they are not two essences, since what is pointed to by *fa-dhālika* is one. As for his saying "the answer to *araʾayta* would be omitted," it is not called an answer; rather it is in the position of the second object of *araʾayta*. As for his saying "Is what he does good?", we do not know of the interrogative hamza entering on *niʿma* or *biʾsa*, because they are expressions of praise and blame, and the interrogative does not enter except on a statement. As for his placing *al-muṣallīn* in the position of the pronoun, and that *al-muṣallīn* is plural because the pronoun of *alladhī yukadhdhibu* means plural, this is clearly forced. The Qurʾān should not be borne except according to what the apparent structure requires. This is the habit of this man: he forces things in understanding the Qurʾān that are not clear.

The discussion of showing off has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqara. The majority read *yurāʾūn* as the present of *raʾā*, on the pattern fāʿala. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Ashhab read it hamzated, shortened, with a doubled hamza. From Ibn Abī Isḥāq: without doubling the hamza. Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Shihāb said: al-māʿūn, in the dialect of Quraysh, is property. al-Farrāʾ said, from some of the Arabs: al-māʿūn is water. *O Caliph of the Merciful, we are a people, upright in faith, who prostrate morning and evening.*

*Arabs whom we see giving from our wealth the right of zakat, sent down as a sending down.*

*A people who, having accepted Islam, have not withheld their māʿūn, nor squandered the tahlīl.*

He means by al-māʿūn zakat, and this view fits both of these. Quṭrub mentioned that its origin is from al-maʿn, which is a small amount, so zakat was called māʿūn because it is a little from much, and likewise ṣadaqa, besides it. ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Religion?﴾ ﴿That is the one who repulses the orphan,﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the poor.﴾ ﴿So woe to those who pray,﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ ﴿who make a show [of their deeds],﴾ ﴿and withhold [simple] assistance.﴾

This surah is Meccan according to the majority. It is Medinan according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda. Hibat Allāh, the blind exegete, said: half of it was revealed in Mecca concerning al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, and half in Medina concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the hypocrite. When God, exalted is He, enumerated His blessings upon the Quraysh, who did not believe in the resurrection and the recompense, He followed His favour to them with a warning of the recompense and a frightening of them with His punishment. It was revealed concerning Abū Jahl, or al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, or al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, or ʿUmar ibn ʿĀʾidh, or two men among the hypocrites, or Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, who used to slaughter a camel every week. An orphan came to him and asked him for something, and he struck him with a stick. These are views, the last of which is that of Ibn Jurayj.

The apparent sense is that *araʾayta* (have you seen) here means "tell me," so it takes two objects. The first is *alladhī* (the one who), and the second is omitted. Al-Ḥawfī supposed it to be: "Is he not deserving of God's punishment?" Al-Zamakhsharī supposed it to be: "Who is he?" That it means "tell me" is shown by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, *araʾaytuka* with the second-person kāf, since the kāf of address does not attach to the sense of seeing. Al-Ḥawfī said: it is also possible that it is from the seeing of the eye, so there would be no omission in the sentence. The interrogative hamza indicates affirmation and making understood, so that the listener may recall whoever is known to him with this description.

Al-dīn (the Religion) means the recompense, by reward and punishment. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is, "Have you recognised the one who denies the recompense? It is he who *repulses the orphan*," that is, pushes him away violently, with harshness or harm. "*And does not urge*," that is, does not stir his household to give food to the poor. He made the knowledge of denying the recompense the cause of withholding kindness and proceeding to harm the weak. End of quote.

The majority read *yadhuʿʿu* with a damma on the dāl and a shadda on the ʿayn. ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ and al-Yamānī read it with a fatḥa on the dāl and no shadda on the ʿayn, meaning he abandons him, that is, does not treat him well and is harsh with him. The majority read *wa-lā yaḥuḍḍu* as the present tense of ḥaḍḍa. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *yuḥāḍḍu*, the present of ḥāḍaḍtu.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: *bi-l-dīn* means "by the judgment of God." Mujāhid said: "by the reckoning." It is also said: "by the recompense," and it is said: "by the Qurʾān." Ibrāhīm ibn ʿArafa said: *yadhuʿʿu al-yatīm* means he pushes him away from his right. Mujāhid said: he pushes him away from his right and does not feed him. In the phrase *wa-lā yaḥuḍḍu* there is an indication that he himself does not feed, once it is assumed, and this is of the category of the more fitting, since if he does not urge others out of stinginess, then it is more fitting and more worthy that he himself abandon it in action. In the addition of *ṭaʿām* (food) to *al-miskīn* (the poor) there is evidence that the poor man is entitled to it.

When He first mentioned the pillar of disbelief, which is denying the Religion, He mentioned what follows from it of what relates to the Creator, which is worshipping Him through prayer, and He said: *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn* (so woe to those who pray). The apparent meaning is that those who pray are other than those previously mentioned. It is said: they are the one who repulses the orphan and not the one who urges. It is also said that each of the blameworthy attributes arises from denying the Religion. So *al-muṣallūn* here, and God knows best, are the hypocrites, to whom prayer is ascribed, meaning the outward forms they perform. Then He said: *alladhīna hum ʿan ṣalātihim sāhūn* (who are heedless of their prayer), considering that they do not perform it as the Muslim performs it, with belief in its obligation and drawing near to God through it. In a hadith concerning *ʿan ṣalātihim sāhūn*: "They delay it beyond its time out of contempt for it." Mujāhid said: it is delay of abandonment and neglect. Ibrāhīm said: it is the one who, when he prostrates, says "with his head like this," turning aside. Qatāda said: it is leaving it, or they are the heedless who do not care whether one of them has prayed or not. Quṭrub said: it is the one who does not settle down and does not remember God, exalted is He. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the hypocrites leave off prayer in secret and perform it openly. *And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily* (Qurʾān 4:142). This shows that it refers to the hypocrites.

His saying, exalted is He: *alladhīna hum yurāʾūn* (who make a show), and this is what Ibn Wahb reported from Mālik. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if He had said *fī ṣalātihim* (in their prayer), it would have applied to the believers. ʿAṭāʾ said: praise be to God, who said *ʿan ṣalātihim* and did not say *fī ṣalātihim*.

Al-Zamakhsharī said, after he had put forward, in what we have quoted from his words, what indicates that *fa-dhālika alladhī yadhuʿʿu* is in the place of the nominative: he said: another way is that *fa-dhālika* is a conjunction with *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, either as the conjunction of one essence to another essence, or as the conjunction of an attribute to an attribute. The answer to *araʾayta* would be omitted, because what follows indicates it. As if he said: "Tell me, and what do you say of one who denies the recompense, and of one who harms the orphan and does not feed the poor? Is what he does good?" Then He said: *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn*, that is, if it is known that he is evil, *fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn*, in the sense of: "woe to them." But He put their description in the place of their pronoun, because they were, along with denying, and what was added to them, heedless of prayer, showing off, and not paying the zakat on their wealth. If you say: how did you make *al-muṣallīn* stand in place of the pronoun of *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, when it is singular? I say: its meaning is plural, because what is meant by it is the genus. End of quote.

So he made *fa-dhālika* in the place of the accusative, as a conjunction with the object. This is a strange construction, like your saying: "I honoured the one who visits us, that is the one who treats us well." What comes first to the mind is that *fa-dhālika* is nominative by being the subject. On the reading of the accusative the sense would be: "I honoured the one who visits us, so I honoured that one who treats us well." The demonstrative in this reading is not as firmly placed as the eloquent usage would have it, since there is no need to point to "the one who visits us." Rather, the eloquent form is "I honoured the one who visits us, so the one who treats us well," or "I honoured the one who visits us, so he treats us well." As for his saying "the conjunction of one essence to another essence," this is not correct, because *fa-dhālika* is a reference to *alladhī yukadhdhibu*, so they are not two essences, since what is pointed to by *fa-dhālika* is one. As for his saying "the answer to *araʾayta* would be omitted," it is not called an answer; rather it is in the position of the second object of *araʾayta*. As for his saying "Is what he does good?", we do not know of the interrogative hamza entering on *niʿma* or *biʾsa*, because they are expressions of praise and blame, and the interrogative does not enter except on a statement. As for his placing *al-muṣallīn* in the position of the pronoun, and that *al-muṣallīn* is plural because the pronoun of *alladhī yukadhdhibu* means plural, this is clearly forced. The Qurʾān should not be borne except according to what the apparent structure requires. This is the habit of this man: he forces things in understanding the Qurʾān that are not clear.

The discussion of showing off has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqara. The majority read *yurāʾūn* as the present of *raʾā*, on the pattern fāʿala. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Ashhab read it hamzated, shortened, with a doubled hamza. From Ibn Abī Isḥāq: without doubling the hamza. The justification of the first is that he doubled the hamza to make it transitive, as they transitivised with the hamza, saying of *raʾā* "arrā," and they said "raʾā," so the present came as *yurawwī*, like *yuṣallī*, and the plural came as *yurawwūn*, like *yuṣallūn*. The justification of the second is that he found the doubling of the hamza heavy and lightened it, or he dropped the alif from *yurāʾūn* without a cause.

*Wa-yamnaʿūna al-māʿūn* (and withhold [simple] assistance). Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Shihāb said: al-māʿūn, in the dialect of Quraysh, is property. al-Farrāʾ said, from some of the Arabs: al-māʿūn is water. Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd said: it is what people give to one another, such as the axe, the bucket and the vessels. In a hadith: "He (ﷺ) was asked about the thing whose withholding is not lawful, and he said: water, salt and fire." In some chains: the needle and the leavening. ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās also said: al-māʿūn is zakat, and from this is the verse of al-Rāʿī:

*O Caliph of the Merciful, we are a people, upright in faith, who prostrate morning and evening.*

*Arabs whom we see giving from our wealth the right of zakat, sent down as a sending down.*

*A people who, having accepted Islam, have not withheld their māʿūn, nor squandered the tahlīl.*

He means by al-māʿūn zakat, and this view fits both of these. Quṭrub mentioned that its origin is from al-maʿn, which is a small amount, so zakat was called māʿūn because it is a little from much, and likewise ṣadaqa, besides it. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is lending of goods. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Kalbī said: it is all kindness. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: withholding what is due. It is also said: water and pasture.
